claims.statement: The SMS gateway is operated from the app's 3-Dots top-bar overflow menu (TopBar renders an 'SMS Gateway' DropdownMenuItem) which opens GatewayScreen, and that screen guides the operator through three steps: enable the gateway (with one-time privacy consent), connect a server (GMweb bridge, cloud backend, or LAN), and share the API key.

The gateway is disabled by default and requires separate, versioned consent (CURRENT_CONSENT_VERSION = 1): the first enable shows an 'Enable SMS Gateway?' dialog (acceptGatewayConsentAndStart records version + timestamp then starts), GatewayService.startGateway re-checks GatewayAccessPolicy.canStart before startForegroundService, and onStartCommand blocks and stopSelfs if consent is missing, so consent is enforced at UI, start entry, and service boundary.

Consent can be revoked at any time from the gateway screen ('Revoke consent and stop Gateway'); revokeGatewayConsent stops the service, clears the consent version, resets gatewayDesiredEnabled/isEnabled/autoStartOnBoot, and clears cloud credentials, so the phone no longer registers, heartbeats, or forwards.

The gateway main switch is bound to the user's intent (gatewayDesiredEnabled) rather than runtime truth so an offline gateway still shows 'on' while waiting for network; the screen polls GatewayService.supervisorState at a 1-second tick and renders state labels ('Gateway Active', 'Waiting for network…', 'Reconnecting…', 'Gateway error — retrying', 'Gateway Stopped'), and 'Reconnect now' calls GatewayService.reconnectNow (supervisor retryNow) plus an optional cloud re-registration when a backend URL is configured.

Gateway API keys are generated as 'gw_' plus 16 random hex bytes (128 bits from a strong RNG via SecureStore.randomHex); the UI supports copy-to-clipboard and regeneration (generateNewApiKey), and the on-screen live log records only a masked form (first 7 + last 4 characters), never the full key.

updateApiKey lets the operator paste a user-supplied key (e.g. the GMweb server's GMWEB_ANDROID_DEVICE_KEY) so phone and server share one secret without copy-pasting in both directions; a blank key is rejected with a toast.

The gateway API key, webhook secret, bearer token, and registration secret are persisted encrypted with the Android Keystore under an 'enc:v1:' prefix, legacy plaintext values are transparently re-encrypted on first read, and the store is fail-closed: storeEncrypted throws (checkNotNull) rather than persisting a secret in plaintext when the Keystore is unavailable.

The embedded gateway HTTP server listens at http://<phone-ip>:8080 by default (DEFAULT_PORT = 8080 in GatewayPreferences) and the gateway screen displays this base URL; the port is persisted in prefs, savePort validates 1024..65535 and notes a restart is needed to apply, and the current GatewayScreen does not render a port input field so 8080 is the practical operating value.

By default GatewayServer.start() binds the socket to the detected LAN IPv4 address (getLocalIpAddress), not 0.0.0.0, to limit exposure to the local network; the 'Bind to all interfaces' switch (bindAllInterfaces) makes it bind to 0.0.0.0 instead, and the change takes effect on the next server start, as logged by saveBindAllInterfaces.

ConnectionSupervisor compares the bound IP against the current LAN IP on a 10-second cadence; when the phone's IPv4 address changes it stops the old server, constructs a fresh GatewayServer, and logs 'LAN address changed (old → new) — rebinding server'; with bindAllInterfaces the bound IP is '0.0.0.0' so the rebind comparison is skipped, and a bind failure (e.g. port taken) puts the supervisor in ERROR with 5 s → 300 s exponential backoff.

The canonical API examples use the X-API-Key header against http://PHONE_IP:8080: POST /api/v1/sms/send with {phone, message} to send now, POST /api/v1/sms/schedule with {phone, message, delaySeconds} for a timed send that survives reboot (WorkManager), and GET /api/v1/sms/schedule/{id} to check (or DELETE to cancel) a scheduled send.

scripts/test-gateway-api.ps1 is a live smoke test for the gateway REST API: it takes -HostIp (default 127.0.0.1, reachable after 'adb forward tcp:8080 tcp:8080' over USB or via the phone's LAN IP), -Port (8080), and a mandatory -ApiKey; the default run is read-only and asserts status=online with ip/port/battery, 401 for wrong and missing keys (missing-key case run last because it counts toward the per-IP brute-force lockout), inbox count<=50 with a messages array, /api/v1/sms limit/offset/type=received filtering, epoch-ms and yyyy-MM-dd date ranges, 400 for blank send fields, 400 for a non-HTTPS imageUrl on /api/v1/mms/send, and 404 for unknown paths; -SendTestSms -To performs live SMS/MMS sends (costing real messages) and the script exits non-zero on any failure.

The README's internet-exposure options are: Cloud backend (zero-setup public URL, default endpoint provided), Cloudflare Tunnel (free stable domain, 'cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8080'), Tailscale (private devices only, no exposed ports, mesh VPN), Port forwarding + DDNS (fixed home WiFi, router config required), and ADB reverse (emulator/testing, 'adb reverse tcp:8080 tcp:8080').

The GMweb pull bridge is an outbound-only HTTPS transport: the operator saves a GMweb server URL (must start with https://; empty disables the bridge) and optionally pastes the server-side key (GMWEB_ANDROID_DEVICE_KEY) which replaces the phone's key so both sides match; the phone then long-polls GET {gmwebUrl}/gateway/pull?waitMs=… (25 s server hold) and acks delivered jobs, needing no tunnel, inbound port, or static IP, with the device appearing online within ~25 s of saving.

The optional cloud relay backend (default https://gaitway.autonomousone.in, settable at build time via -PGATEWAY_BACKEND_URL) lets the phone register and send periodic heartbeats (battery, signal, queue depth) while the Gateway Service is enabled so external projects reach it at a fixed HTTPS URL; the backendUrl preference enforces https:// (rejecting http) so the bearer token is never sent over plaintext, and nothing is transmitted unless the user enables the service.

In the current GatewayScreen the GMweb card, server-status card (base URL + bind switch), REST-endpoints card, and live-logs card are visible, while the Cloud backend card, API-key-auth card, and Incoming SMS Webhook card are wired but hidden behind the showAdvancedGatewayModes = false flag; the REST-endpoints card shows a Cloud Mode / LAN Mode badge with the effective base URL (backend URL when cloud-connected, else http://<local-ip>:<port>) and a LAN fallback address.

Incoming SMS are POSTed as JSON to the configured webhook endpoint; when a signing secret (stored Keystore-encrypted) is set, WebhookEngine signs the payload with HMAC-SHA256 over '<timestamp>.<body>' sent as the X-Signature header (with X-Timestamp) for authenticity and replay rejection, a blank secret disables signing, and blocked numbers never trigger webhooks.

DiagnosticLog never records SMS bodies or full phone numbers; it records state transitions and raw numeric result codes, and every logged message is sanitized by replacing 7–15 digit sequences (optionally + prefixed, not embedded in a longer alphanumeric run) with 'phone#<token>' where the token is the first 5 bytes of SHA-256 of the number hex-encoded (truncating to 24,000 chars first); the broad pattern may redact long numeric ids, which the code comment says is preferred to leaking a number.

DiagnosticLog files live in app-private storage (<filesDir>/diagnostics/): the current file messages-diagnostics.log rotates when it reaches 384*1024 bytes, keeping 3 generations (rotate deletes the oldest, shifts the rest, current becomes .1), bounding retained history at ~1.15 MB; write failures are swallowed to a Log.w so diagnostics never break the app.

DiagnosticLog.initialize is called from MessagesApp.onCreate, which also installs a default uncaught-exception handler that writes DiagnosticLog.event('CRASH', …) with the full stack trace before delegating to the previous handler, so crashes are captured on-device even though logcat may rotate past them.

Diagnostics export is user-initiated: Settings → Data tools → 'Export diagnostic log' calls DiagnosticLog.createExportFile, which logs a 'user requested export' event and writes a merged snapshot (messages-diagnostics-<ts>.txt) to the cache dir with a header stating 'SMS bodies and full phone numbers are intentionally excluded.', appending generations oldest-first with '===== <file> =====' separators, then shares it via FileProvider ACTION_SEND (no storage permission); the gateway screen separately offers a live server-log feed (last 100 lines) with a share button.

BackupRepository backs up and restores SMS in Android-compatible XML with the same shape as the classic 'SMS Backup & Restore' app (<smses count="N"> with <sms address/body/date/dateSent/read/type/status/threadId/> attributes), so backups are portable between apps and human-readable; backupTo streams all rows in ascending date order omitting _ID so restored rows get new ids, and both run from Settings → Data tools (SAF CreateDocument with suggested name messages-backup.xml for backup; OpenDocument with a confirmation dialog for restore).

SMS restore is additive (inserts rows, never replaces or wipes, per the confirm dialog 'Existing messages are kept'); each <sms> maps to ContentValues with defaults (read→1, status→-1, date→0 when missing), rows lacking an address attribute are skipped, a failing insert is logged and the rest continue, THREAD_ID is deliberately dropped so the provider recomputes it (device-specific), and SmsRepository.notifyExternalChange() refreshes the UI afterwards.

'Export all chats' (ExportRepository.exportAllChats) exports every SMS conversation as a single JSON document (app, exportedAt, conversationCount, messageCount, conversations[] with type/sender/message/date/dateSent/status per message) grouped by thread id (falling back to address) and sorted by date, written to the cache dir and shared via FileProvider without a storage permission; like the XML backup it covers the SMS provider only, so MMS rows/media are not part of either archive.

'Delete messages by period' bulk-deletes before or after a chosen date across both providers: deleteSmsByRange filters Telephony.Sms.DATE in milliseconds while deleteMmsByRange filters Telephony.Mms.DATE in seconds (cutoffMillis / 1000 to compensate); the operation requires default-SMS-app status, reports 'Deleted N SMS, M MMS', and a provider failure returns -1 for that count without aborting the other.
